findings.title: Arcade Rush always grades A: zero cabinets earns a gold A and a bonus star
findings.problem: In rush mode the time limit is 190 s (`limits.time=RUSH_TIME+10`) and the shift always ends at exactly 180 s. The time axis is therefore always A, and Good Job grading takes the overall grade as the best of the three axes. The result is an A however the shift went. I ran the shift twice. In the first run Pip never sat at the bench. The result card showed 'Orders served: 0', the rows 3:00 A / 0 A / 0 A, a big gold A with a star and a green check, confetti, and the bonus 'Fuse tripped no more than once' lit. In the second run nine cabinets were fixed elegantly, and the card was identical apart from the count. The number of cabinets served, which is the whole point of the mode, does not affect the grade. The cost axis works against success: `spent` grows with every signed-off block (limit 24), so a strong player who fixes 40 cabinets reaches cost 67 (grade D), and that axis is hidden behind the time A. The lobby records this A as the door medal, so the medal teaches the player that the mode doesn't matter. Nothing rewards applying I = (V−Vf)/R quickly and correctly, which kills the rush's reason to exist as practice.
evidence: src/ui/game-ui.ts:216-217 ('Orders served' only text, not graded)
mockups/review5/tools/arcade-rush-teach/result.mjs output: idle → '0 served 3:00 A 0 A 0 A', good → '9 served 3:00 A 0 A 14 A'
findings.fix: Add an optional `grade?():{parts:Grade[];overall:Grade}` to the Station interface (src/stations/types.ts) and have game.ts:354 use it when present. For the arcade in rush mode, grade three rush axes: (1) cabinets fixed: A ≥ 8, B ≥ 5, C ≥ 3, otherwise D; (2) mistakes per cabinet: A ≤ 0.25, B ≤ 0.5, C ≤ 1; (3) elegant share: A ≥ 60 %, B ≥ 30 %. Take the overall grade from the cabinet count, capped one letter above the worst of the other two, so wrecking or idling can't earn an A. Show these rows on the result card instead of time/damage/cost when `rushStatus()` exists. Make every rush bonus need `served.length>0` (the 'Fuse tripped no more than once' ok() at station.ts:116 should be `this.served.length>0&&this.trips<=1`).
findings.verify: Re-run mockups/review5/tools/arcade-rush-teach/result.mjs idle: the card shows D and no lit bonus. Re-run `result.mjs good` (9 cabinets): the card shows A. Add a unit test that a rush station with served=[] grades D.
findings.verify_reason: Code: grade.ts:5-6 takes overall=[...parts].sort()[0], which is the BEST letter. In rush, station.ts:108 sets limits.time=190, and complete() (station.ts:487) ends at game.time>=180, so the time axis is always A and the overall grade is always A. game-ui.ts:217 shows 'Orders served' only as text, and won() records result.overall via record() (game-ui.ts:209), so the lobby medal is always A. Screenshot arcade-rush-teach-43 shows 0 served, rows 3:00 A / 0 A / 0 A, a gold A with a star and a check, and the 'Fuse tripped no more than once' bonus lit, because station.ts:116 has no served>0 guard. One detail is wrong: with cost limit 24, rank() gives D only above 72, so 67 is C, not D. 40 cabinets in 180 s is also unrealistic with a 2 s soak. The conclusion stands.
extra_evidence: src/stations/arcade/station.ts:116 (trips<=1 has no served guard, so it is lit on an idle run)
findings.fix_correction: The fix is sound. Correct the example: cost 67 against limit 24 is C (D needs >72). Keep the rush grade inside the Station.grade() hook and don't change grade.ts globally: the best-of-three rule is shared by every other level.

findings.title: Rush 'Too bright, and the block smells warm' story is false in two thirds of cases: the fuse trips or the LED pops instead
findings.problem: The 'hot' fault always starts with a single 47 Ω block whatever the supply, and always shows the story 'Too bright, and the block smells warm.' I computed read() over 2000 generated jobs. In 261 of the 389 'hot' cabinets (67 %) the start setup trips the 100 mA fuse (9 V and 12 V: 125–208 mA) or pops the LED (5 V red/green: 62.5 mA > 2.5 × 20 mA). The player never sees a 'too bright' LED or a warm block. The very first rush cabinet with this seed (White LED on 9 V) is one of them. The story describes a symptom, the player powers on, and gets 'TRIP' and '47 Ω lets 125 mA through: the fuse tripped.' The text and the world contradict each other. A learner can't build the link between symptom and cause (too bright means too little resistance; fuse trip means far too little) when the stated symptom is wrong. This breaks the rule that failures must be truthful and readable from the world.
evidence: src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:215 (hot fault: chain [[47]] for every supply)
mockups/review5/tools/arcade-rush-teach/jobs.mjs output: hotStoryMismatch 261/389, job 0 startI 125 mA tripped
mockups/review5/shots/arcade-rush-teach-03-bench-job0-start.jpg (story 'Too bright, and the block smells warm.')
findings.fix: In rushJob (logic.ts:212-218), build the 'hot' start so that its reading really is too bright and not destructive. Search the single blocks and two-block chains for the largest R whose read() has `!tripped && 1 < level < HOUSE.ledPop*0.9` and whose block heat lies in 0.6–1.0. If none exists, fall back to a 'trips' fault with the story 'The fuse keeps cutting out.' Better still, derive every story from read(job,start) rather than from the fault label: tripped → 'The fuse keeps cutting out.'; level > ledPop → 'Its light flashed and died; a spare is in.'; iLoad > imax → 'Glaring, and the block smells warm.'; under the band → 'Dimmer than the others.'; reversed → 'Stays dark.'
findings.verify: Add a logic.test.ts case: for 500 rushJob()s with a 'Too bright' story, read(start) has !tripped and 1 < level < 2.5. Retake shots 03/04 for the first cabinet: the story matches what powering on shows.
findings.verify_reason: logic.ts:215 always starts the 'hot' fault as [[47]] with the 'Too bright…' story. My independent run of 2000 jobs (same seed) gives 393 'hot' jobs: 222 trip the fuse and 58 pop the LED, 280/393 = 71% (the reviewer had 67% on a different count). In game, job 0 (White LED on 9 V) tripped on the first power-on with the story still reading 'Too bright, and the block smells warm.' (play.mjs log 'job0 power .3': toast '47 Ω lets 125 mA through: the fuse tripped.'). Screenshot arcade-rush-teach-04 matches. Even the non-destructive cases barely warm the block: 47 Ω at 42 mA is about 33% of ¼ W, so 'smells warm' is weak too.

findings.title: An LED that pops says it 'runs hot and dies early'
findings.problem: When the LED is driven past 2.5 × its rating it pops after 0.5 s. There is a flash and a puff, the power cuts, and a spare goes in. The toast for this event is `judge(...).problems[0]`, which for any over-rating LED reads '62.5 mA is over the LED's 20 mA rating: it runs hot and dies early. (I = (V − Vf) ÷ R)'. The game has just shown instant death, and the sentence describes slow wear. The two failure modes the arcade carefully separates (over-rating shortens life; a gross overload kills at once, logic.ts:14) get the same words exactly when the difference is visible. A learner concludes either that 'dies early' means 'pops now' or that the text is decoration. In rush this happens on every 5 V red or green 'hot' cabinet (job 4 with this seed).
evidence: rush2.mjs log 'job4 .65': mis 1, spent +1, powered false, toast '…runs hot and dies early'
findings.fix: Give popLed its own sentence, built from the reading: `${mA(r.iLoad)} mA is ${(r.level).toFixed(1)}× the LED's ${mAr(imax)} mA rating: that far over, it burns out at once.` Keep 'runs hot and dies early' for 1×–2.5×. Optionally add the ratio to the over-rating message ('1.1× its rating: it runs hot and dies early') so the scale reads as one rule.
findings.verify: Re-run rush2.mjs and retake shot 23: the toast says 'burns out at once'. Add a station spec: red LED on 5 V with 47 Ω → after the pop, the toast contains 'at once'.
findings.verify_reason: station.ts:307-309: popLed toasts judge().problems[0]. For a lit LED over imax that string is logic.ts:158, '…it runs hot and dies early.' Screenshot arcade-rush-teach-23 (viewed) shows exactly that toast right after the pop, with the LED gone and the bench off. The text describes slow wear while the world shows instant death, which contradicts the guardrail in logic.ts:14.

findings.title: A third of rush cabinets need no resistor reasoning, and the stories print the diagnosis
findings.problem: rushJob only rejects starts with tier ≥ 2, so tier-1 'Works' starts are allowed (and logic.test.ts asserts `<2`, not `===0`). Over 2000 jobs, 14 % of cabinets can be signed off exactly as found: power on, wait 2 s, press Enter. The 'Barely glowing… looks broken' cabinet at 7.1 mA passes the play test and is signed off 'Works'. Another 21 % are the 'backwards' fault, which starts with the elegant chain already in place: one F press gives an elegant ★. So about 35 % of the shift is solved without choosing a single resistor. The stories also name the fault outright: 'Someone fitted a block across the LED', 'Right blocks, but the LED went in backwards', 'The chain socket is empty'. The diagnostic skill (reading a symptom such as dark, fuse cutting out, glaring or dim, and mapping it to a cause) is done for the player by text. This breaks 'play by doing, not reading' and the failure rule 'show why, never print the fix': for these faults the cause *is* the fix.
evidence: mockups/review5/shots/arcade-rush-teach-21-job1-dim-close.jpg ('Works: 7.09 mA is under the 8–16 mA band' after signing off untouched)
findings.fix: (1) logic.ts:219: `if(judge(job,job.start).tier>=1)continue;`, and change logic.test.ts:83 to `.toBe(0)`. (2) 'backwards' start: use a chain that is also off-band (for example the fix with one block swapped for its neighbour value), so the player must flip AND choose. Or flip the LED on a random fault so polarity is one of two problems. (3) Make the stories symptom-only (see the 'Too bright' finding): 'Stays dark.', 'The fuse keeps cutting out.', 'Glaring.', 'Dimmer than the others.' The across-block and the empty socket can then be spotted on the board, which is the skill. (4) Optional: in rush, refuse sign-off below tier 2 with a short 'hm' and the meter's band highlighted, so 'Works' isn't a shortcut.
findings.verify: Rerun stats.mjs: tier1Frac 0 and no 'backwards' job whose start chain equals best(). Retake shot 21: Enter is refused or the start is not signable. Unit test: no rush story contains 'across', 'backwards' or 'empty'.
findings.verify_reason: logic.ts:219 rejects only tier>=2 starts, and logic.test.ts:83 asserts toBeLessThan(2). My stats: tier1 starts 280/2000 = 14% (all of them 'dim' jobs), backwards 416/2000 = 20.8%. The 'backwards' start is fix.map(...) (logic.ts:214), so a single flip gives an elegant result. In game I powered job 1 (Red 12 V, 3×470) as found, the play test passed, and Enter signed it off ('Racer: Works', served 2) without touching a block (play.mjs 'job1 signed as found'; shot verify-…-03). The stories name the faults verbatim (logic.ts:213-217). Caveat on fix part (4): refusing sign-off at tier 1 would contradict the Works/Reliable/Elegant ladder used everywhere else. Rejecting tier-1 starts at generation (part 1) already removes the shortcut.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/tools/verify-arcade-rush-teach/play.mjs log 'job1 signed as found' (served 2, no block changed)
mockups/review5/shots/verify-arcade-rush-teach-03-job1-soakdone-hover-D.jpg ('Works: 7.09 mA is under the 8–16 mA band' with PLAY TEST PASSED)
docs/PROGRESS.md:215 claims 'Every generated cabinet starts broken', which is contradicted
findings.fix_correction: Drop part (4), refusing sign-off below tier 2. Tier 1 'Works' is a valid Good Job pass across the game. Parts (1)-(3) are enough. Generating starts with tier 0 only (test .toBe(0)) removes the as-found shortcut.

findings.title: Trial and error is free and fast: the live meter plus free block swaps make guessing beat computing
findings.problem: Rush should be where the player applies R = (V − Vf)/I under time pressure, but nothing rewards predicting. Swapping blocks while powered costs nothing: `spent` only adds the signed-off setup's blocks. The meter updates current at once. A tier-0 setup only counts as a mistake after running 0.6 s, so quick swaps are free. Over 300 rush jobs, a random one- or two-block chain is reliable 25 % of the time and elegant 11 %. Eleven chains cover every answer, and five of them (470, 470+470, 220, 220+470, 220‖470) cover 71 %. In my scripted brute-force run (job 9: 47, 100, 220, 470, 220+47, 100+100 with power on) six guesses cost one mistake, and the elegant 220 was found by sweeping. Red and green LEDs (Vf 2.0 and 2.1 V) give the same answer in 7 of 12 supply and band combinations. Supplies are always 3.3, 5, 9 or 12 V, so after a few minutes the player memorises '9 V → 470' instead of the relation.
evidence: stats.mjs output: relFrac 0.248, eleFrac 0.1085, 11 distinct fixes, redGreenSame 7/12
rush2.mjs log 'job9 try …' (six tries, mistakes 3→4 only on 47 Ω)
findings.fix: Make prediction the scoring mechanic. (a) Track `powerOns` per cabinet and store `first:boolean` in `served` when the first power-on was already in the band. Add a rush bonus 'Five cabinets right on the first power-on' and count first-try cabinets on the result card. (b) In rush, treat changing a block while powered as a hot swap: a small spark and a mistake (real bench practice: power off before rework). Together with a PTC that latches until power-off (see the PTC finding) this is truthful. (c) Widen the inputs so memorising fails: supplies from [3.3, 3.7 (Li-ion), 5, 6, 9, 12, 24] and bands from 5–20 mA in 1 mA steps, keeping `best()` solvable. Raise the 'reliable' bar so it needs the margin, not luck.
findings.verify: Scripted sweep (like rush2.mjs job 9) at the bench: swapping while live adds mistakes. A first-try run shows the bonus lit. Rerun stats.mjs: no single fix above 15 % of jobs.
findings.verify_reason: The mechanics are confirmed in code. spent grows only at sign-off (station.ts:273) or on a pop (300, 308). A tier-0 setup is counted only after runT>0.6 s (390), and changed() resets runT on every swap (247), so quick swaps cost nothing. Only trips, after 0.15 s, are counted. Answer concentration is confirmed and stronger than reported: in my 2000 jobs, 11 distinct fixes, and the top 5 (220+470 25.4%, 470 13.9%, 220 13.6%, 470+470 13.3%, 220‖470 12.0%) cover 78%. That guessing beats computing for real players is a reasonable inference but I did not measure it. Fix (b) is a problem: making every live swap a spark and a mistake punishes experimentation, which contradicts finding 5 and the forgiving-interaction rule.
extra_evidence: src/stations/arcade/station.ts:247 (changed() resets runT/explained/faultCounted on every swap)
findings.fix_correction: Drop (b), the hot-swap mistake. It punishes trying things and conflicts with the 'experiments are not damage' direction (review4 DESIGN_A.md:224/243 and finding 5). Keep (a), reward a first power-on in the band (a bonus plus a count on the card), and (c), widen supplies and bands so no single fix exceeds about 15%.

findings.title: Looking at a fault costs damage: powering on 'as found' counts a mistake and a fuse trip on half of all rush cabinets
findings.problem: Over 2000 generated jobs, 50 % of starts trip the fuse on power-on (empty socket, across-block, 47 Ω on 9 or 12 V), and 3 % pop the LED. The natural diagnostic move, 'switch it on and see what's wrong', counts a mistake and a trip through `fault(true)`. The rush damage limit is 3, and the bonus 'Fuse tripped no more than once' is gone after the first look. In my run, the first press of POWER on cabinet 1 gave mistakes 1 and trips 1. This is review 4's A7 (experiments graded as damage) and it is worse in rush, because the generator makes tripping starts common. It punishes the inquiry the game should teach (observe the symptom, then reason), and it pushes players to never power on until they have guessed.
findings.fix: Add `touched=false` per cabinet, set true in act() for pick, slot or flip and reset in signoff (station.ts:277). In fault() and popLed()/popBlock(), skip counting mistakes and trips while `!this.touched`, so the setup as found is a free look. Keep the click, sparks, TILT marquee and toast so the symptom still shows. Phrase that first toast as diagnosis ('As found: it trips the fuse').
findings.verify: rush.mjs: power on cabinet 0 as found → snap().station.mistakes===0 and trips===0. Then build 47 Ω yourself and power on → mistakes 1. Add a station-arcade-rush spec case.
findings.verify_reason: Reproduced: power on job 0 as found → snapshot mis 1, trips 1 after 0.3 s (play.mjs 'job0 power .3'). fault(true) is called from trip() (station.ts:285-288) with no check for whether the player changed anything. My stats: 1010/2000 starts (50.5%) trip and 58 (2.9%) pop. The 'Fuse tripped no more than once' bonus (station.ts:116) is therefore lost on the second cabinet the player merely looks at. This repeats review4 DESIGN_A.md:224 ('Experiments are graded as damage').

findings.title: The 'PTC fuse' re-arms while powered and keeps re-tripping; real polymer PTCs latch until power is removed
findings.problem: Still open from the research lead (A-1); the rush story leans on it ('The fuse keeps clicking'). The fuse cools whether or not the bench is on and conducts again after 2.5 s. With the fault still in place it trips again: in my run cabinet 0 was still or again tripped 3.2 s after power-on with the bench left on. That is a bimetal auto-reset breaker. A polymer PTC stays latched (high resistance, held hot by a small leakage current) until the fault is cleared AND power is removed (Littelfuse technical paper; Wikipedia 'Resettable fuse'). It also adds dead time: after fixing the chain the player must wait out 'FUSE COOLING 1.4 s' even though the circuit is now fine. That is a locked wait inside a 3-minute shift, repeated on every tripping cabinet. The red-hot halo is also untruthful: a PPTC trips at about 125 °C and doesn't glow.
evidence: rush.mjs log 'job0 after 3.2 s': tripped true while powered
findings.fix: Take option (b) from the lead: in update(), count `cooling` down only while `!this.powered`. Keep `tripped` latched while powered, and show the prompt 'P Power off to reset the fuse'. Shorten fuseCool to 1.0 s in rush (power-off is now the cost, which teaches 'remove power before rework'). Replace the red halo with a warm amber tint (#ffb347, halo opacity ≤ 0.3). Rename the rush story to 'The fuse keeps cutting out.'
findings.verify: New station spec: a tripping chain with power left on is still tripped after 5 s. Power off for 1 s, then on with a correct chain → live. Retake shot 26: no cooling wait after power-cycling.
findings.verify_reason: The behaviour is real. station.ts:374 cools the fuse while powered, and with the fault in place it re-trips: still tripped 3.2 s after power-on with the bench on (play.mjs 'job0 after 3.2 s powered'). After I fixed the chain to 470 Ω while tripped, it was still 'fuse cooling' (play.mjs 'job0 fixed while tripped', shot verify-…-02), so there is a wait of up to 2.5 s. The physics is right too: a polymer PTC latches while voltage is applied. I lowered the priority because the player never sees the word 'PTC'. The board says 'FUSE' and the meter 'FUSE COOLING' (grep: PTC appears only in code comments). An auto-reset breaker that clicks and cycles (a bimetal thermal breaker) behaves exactly as shown, so what the player learns ('it trips, cools, conducts again') is not false at the level taught. The yellow-disc model does look like a PPTC, and the red glow is untruthful for either device. The rest is mainly the dead-time wait.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/tools/verify-arcade-rush-teach/play.mjs logs 'job0 after 3.2 s powered' (tr true) and 'job0 fixed while tripped' (470 Ω, tr true)
grep: 'PTC' appears only in comments (logic.ts:13,28; station.ts:2,8,84,151,286,373), never in player-facing text
mockups/review5/research-external.md:152-155 (F6, already reported P key/power confusion while tripped)
findings.fix_correction: Either option is truthful. (a) The reviewer's latching PTC: cool only while !powered, prompt 'P Power off to reset'. Or (b) the cheaper fix: keep the cycling and treat it as a bimetal auto-reset breaker, change the disc model to a small metal-can breaker, and fix the comments. Either way, drop the red-hot glow and let a fixed chain clear the trip on the next power-cycle without waiting out the full fuseCool.

findings.title: An overdriven LED looks paler and weaker than a correctly driven one, and the LED HEAT bar barely moves before it pops
findings.problem: The core intuition is that more current means a brighter, hotter LED. At 7.1 mA (well under the band) the red LED dome is saturated red with a clear halo. At 62.5 mA (3×) the dome is lerped toward white, up to 70 %, and reads pale pink-white, with a broad orange wash from the point light over the whole board. The over-driven LED reads as washed out, not glaring. Separately, the pop is triggered by current (`r.level > ledPop` for 0.5 s), but the LED HEAT bar follows a 2 s thermal time constant. At 0.3 s it showed 33 °C, and the LED popped at 0.65 s with the heat bar still low. The meter the player is told to watch never shows the cause before the failure.
evidence: src/stations/arcade/station.ts:403-408 (lerp to white, `over` flicker, ledLight intensity)
src/stations/arcade/station.ts:380, :386 (heat lags with tau 2 s; pop on level after .5 s)
findings.fix: In animate(): keep the LED's hue (no lerp to white). Express overdrive as glare: halo scale `.4+min(3,level)*.6`, a bloom-only core, a slight size pulse and the flicker, and cap the board wash (ledLight distance 0.8, intensity ≤ 2). Give the LED its own fast thermal constant (`HOUSE.ledTau=.25`) and trigger the pop from `heat.led > HOUSE.ledPop`. Rescale the LED HEAT bar to 0–3× with a red 'burn-out' zone above 2.5×, so the bar visibly races into the red before the pop.
findings.verify: Crop the LED at 7 mA, 18 mA and 62 mA: halo size increases monotonically and the hue stays red. In a frame sequence of the 62 mA case, LED HEAT reaches the red zone before the pop. Unit test: the pop needs heat.led > 2.5.
findings.verify_reason: The visual is confirmed. Shot arcade-rush-teach-20 (7.09 mA) shows a saturated red dome. Shot 22 (62.5 mA at 0.3 s) shows a pale pink-white dome and an orange wash over the board. LED HEAT reads 33 °C with its bar far below the limit line, and the pop is triggered from r.level (station.ts:386), not from heat.led. The stated cause is partly wrong. At 0.3 s heat.led = 3.125·(1−e^−0.15) ≈ 0.44, and even at the 0.65 s pop it is about 0.87, below the 0.9 'over' threshold, so the lerp toward white (station.ts:407) is NOT active in the pop case. The washout comes from multiplyScalar(.6+glowK*1.1) = 2.36 on a tone-mapped MeshBasicMaterial (unlitMat, toneMapped defaults to true): ACES pushes the over-range red toward white. ledLight.intensity = 4.8 causes the board wash. The lerp does apply for sustained overdrive below the pop (e.g. 5 V blue at 2.08×).
extra_evidence: src/stations/arcade/station.ts:570 (LED HEAT bar uses m.led, limit line at 1, max 1.5)
findings.fix_correction: Also cap the dome colour multiplier at about 1.1–1.2, or set ledOn.toneMapped=false with a clamped colour, so the hue holds. Removing the lerp alone won't fix the pop case, because the lerp isn't active there. Express overdrive through halo size and bloom, and cap ledLight intensity at about 2 with distance 0.8. The LED-heat or pop-trigger change is as proposed.

findings.title: LED-pop smoke is a giant grey ball that covers the LED, the meter and half the board
findings.problem: When the LED pops, the smoke burst (10 'smoke' particles at the LED) shows from the bench camera as one huge translucent grey sphere, about 450 px across. It hides the LED being taught, the right half of the meter (light, heat, fuse readouts) and the ACROSS slot, right when the player needs to see what happened and read the toast. It reads as a rendering glitch rather than a puff.
findings.fix: Use bench-scale smoke for station effects. Add a `scale` option to game.burst (or a 'wisp' kind) and call it from popLed/popBlock with 4 puffs of start radius ≤ 0.04 m, rising 0.3 m, opacity ≤ 0.45, fading within 0.8 s. Also offset them slightly away from the camera (−z board-local) so they rise behind the LED.
findings.verify: Retake shot 23 (rush2.mjs, job 4 at +0.65 s): the LED dome and the meter's light/heat rows stay legible, and the smoke covers less than 10 % of the board.
findings.verify_reason: Shot arcade-rush-teach-23 (viewed) shows a single grey translucent sphere, roughly 450 px wide, covering the LED, the ACROSS slot and the right half of the meter. Cause: particles.ts:31-34 makes each 'smoke' puff an ico(1) of size 0.14–0.22 m that grows to 3.4× (particles.ts:48), so about 0.5–0.75 m radius each. Ten of them at one point (station.ts:311) merge into a ball at bench scale. popBlock (station.ts:303, 8 puffs) and the hot-block smoke (station.ts:421) use the same kind. I lowered it to P2: it lasts about 1.5 s, the toast below stays legible, and the bench is already powered off at that moment, so no live reading is hidden.
extra_evidence: src/stations/arcade/station.ts:303, :421 (same smoke kind for block pops and hot blocks)

findings.title: The hover hint overrides the step prompt, and 'P Fuse cooling' labels a key that powers off
findings.problem: prompt() returns the hover hint before any step prompt. With the mouse resting over pad D (where it lands after the camera zoom, and a common resting spot), the prompt read 'D Empty: plain wire' through the trip, the LED pop, the play test and the 'ready to sign off' state. The player is never shown 'Enter Sign off' and can wait for nothing while the rush clock runs. Separately, while the fuse is tripped the prompt is 'P Fuse cooling'. P doesn't cool the fuse, it powers the bench off, so the key and the text disagree.
findings.fix: In prompt(), put `if(this.soakDone)return {key:'Enter',text:'Sign off'}` and the tripped state before the hover hint. Only use the hover hint if the pointer moved within the last 1.5 s (store `lastPointerT` in pointer()). Change the tripped prompt to `{key:'P',text:'Power off (fuse tripped)'}`, matching the latching-PTC fix.
findings.verify: Retake shot 28 with the mouse over pad D: the prompt reads 'Enter Sign off'. Shot 04: the prompt reads 'P Power off…'.
findings.verify_reason: Reproduced. With the mouse resting over pad D and the play test passed (soakDone true, sign-off button lit green), the prompt read 'D Take a block out'. Moving the mouse away changed it to 'Enter Sign off' (play.mjs logs 'job1 as found soak' / 'job1 mouse moved away'; shot verify-…-03). The tripped prompt is 'P Fuse cooling' (play.mjs 'job0 power .3'), and P powers off. I lowered it to P2: other cues remain when the hover hint wins (the sign-off button turns green, the meter shows 'PLAY TEST PASSED ✓', and the toast gives the verdict), so the player is not stuck. The P-key mismatch was already reported as research-external F6 (P2).
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/shots/verify-arcade-rush-teach-03-job1-soakdone-hover-D.jpg (viewed: 'D Take a block out' while PLAY TEST PASSED)
mockups/review5/tools/verify-arcade-rush-teach/play.mjs logs 'job1 as found soak' vs 'job1 mouse moved away'

findings.title: The success consequence is off-screen: the play-test kid and the cabinet lamp sit outside the bench camera
findings.problem: The design says a kid plays each cabinet while it runs in spec, hopping, cheering or slumping, and the cabinet's lamp, screen and 'TILT!' marquee react. All of these live on the serviced cabinet at the bench's left end (x = table − 2.95). The bench camera (distance 5.9, pitch 0.98) frames only the bins, board, meter and lever. In every bench screenshot only a sliver of pink cabinet shows at the far left edge. The kid and the TILT marquee are never seen. In rush the player spends nearly the whole shift at the bench, so success and failure appear only as a meter bar and a toast. The 'show it in the world' half of the lesson is missing.
findings.fix: Bring the cabinet into frame. Either move it to sit behind the bins at about (t.x+OX−1.9, t.z−.9) facing the camera, with the kid on its front side, or widen the bench view (`view={distance:6.8,pitch:.9,lookY:.35}`) and shift the bench contents right (OX=.15). The marquee, cabinet lamp and kid should all be inside the frame at 1440×900. Keep the toast area clear of them.
findings.verify: Bench screenshot at power-on in spec: the kid is visible and hopping. On a trip, the TILT marquee is visible in the same frame.
findings.verify_reason: The bench camera is fixed. A right-drag orbit of −400 px and a wheel zoom of +600 at the bench left the framing unchanged (shots verify-arcade-rush-teach-04/05 match the default bench view). The serviced cabinet with the kid and the marquee sits at t.x+OX−2.75 = −2.95 (station.ts:215), shown only as a pink sliver at the far left edge in every bench shot (arcade-rush-teach-04, -20, -22). In the room view (verify-…-01) the cabinet and kid stand just left of the bench, so they exist but are never framed while the player works. The play-test kid and the TILT marquee are therefore invisible during rush.
extra_evidence: mockups/review5/shots/verify-arcade-rush-teach-01-start-clock.jpg (cabinet+kid visible beside the bench in room view)

findings.title: The rush clock runs during a repeated tray fetch, before the player knows it has started
findings.problem: Rush uses game.time from spawn. The HUD reads 2:59 at the first frame, while the card still says 'Carry the tray of resistor blocks from the storeroom…'. The player must redo the Arcade's tray carry, which they have already done (rush is locked until the Arcade is finished). With my scripted ideal route Pip reached the bench at 171 s left; a human route costs 15–25 s. This is dead time with nothing to learn, eats about 10 % of the shift, and isn't signposted as part of the timed run.
evidence: rush.mjs log 'bench': t 9.5 s, panel 'RUSH · 171 s'
findings.fix: In rush, start with `trayReady=true`, bins visible and the tray removed, spawn Pip at (0.6, −0.6) beside the bench, and drop the carry step. Alternatively, keep the walk but start the countdown on the first setActive(true): store `rushStart=this.game.time` and use `time−rushStart` in current(), complete() and rushStatus(). Show 'Sit at the bench to start the clock' until then.
findings.verify: snap() at the moment of sitting shows rushStatus().left === 180. The station-arcade-rush spec still passes with the route shortened.
findings.verify_reason: Code: rush uses game.time from spawn (station.ts:127, :487-489), and the rush steps include the carry (station.ts:109-112). Screenshot verify-…-01 shows 2:59 with the carry card at t = 0.2. My scripted ideal route reached the bench at t = 6.5 s (play.mjs 'at bench'), faster than the reviewer's 9.5 s. A human route is plausibly 15–25 s. I lowered it to P2: the HUD clock is visible and counting from frame one, so it is signposted. The walk is a few seconds of the 180 s shift, and while finding 0 stands the count doesn't even affect the grade. It becomes more important once rush grades on cabinets.

findings.title: P = I²R never decides a rush cabinet: block heat and parallel heat-sharing are untested
findings.problem: The Arcade teaches series, parallel, P = I²R against a ¼ W rating with a 60 % house margin, battery life and base drive. Rush generates only LED cabinets whose elegant fix runs its hottest block at no more than about 32 % of rating (fixHeat 0.03–0.32 across the sampled jobs). The ¼ W rating and the 60 % rule never bind, and a side-by-side pair is only ever needed to hit a resistance value, never to share heat. Rush also has no battery cabinets and no transistor base. The 3-minute drill exercises only one formula and one trap, with no escalation over the shift. The heat half of the lesson gets no moment of application.
evidence: jobs.mjs output: fixHeat ≤ 0.32 for all 16 jobs
findings.fix: Escalate within the shift. Cabinets 1–4 use the current generator. From cabinet 5, mix in 'hot rail' LED cabinets (24 V supply or a 30–40 mA band with imax raised for a high-power LED), where any single block that meets the band runs above 60 % of ¼ W, so only a parallel pair or a series split passes reliably. From cabinet 8, add battery cabinets with a life target (≥ 30 h) and occasional base-drive cabinets (reusing JOBS[4]'s Base load). Keep the `best()` solvability check. Reflect the new idea in the story ('Bright one: its block keeps scorching').
findings.verify: Unit test: for rushJob n ≥ 4, at least 25 % of jobs have a single-block solution that fails the margin (tier ≤ 1) and a pair solution that is tier 3. Rerun jobs.mjs and check fixHeat.
findings.verify_reason: Rush is LED-only (logic.ts:204-221), with no battery or base cabinets and no escalation. That is confirmed. The claim that the ¼ W rating and the 60% rule 'never bind' is overstated. Over 2000 jobs the elegant fix runs its hottest block at up to 40% (not 32%), and in 57/300 jobs (19%) some in-band chain fails the 60% margin (e.g. a single 470 near the top of the band on 12 V). So the margin can decide a Reliable-vs-Works verdict. It never forces a side-by-side pair for heat. This is a content-scope request for a drill mode, not a defect in what is taught, so P2.
findings.fix_correction: Correct the premise: the margin does bind on about 19% of jobs for near-top-of-band chains. It never forces a parallel pair. The escalation idea is fine as a P2 enhancement.

findings.title: 'Barely glowing… looks broken' at 7 mA, while the game's own lit threshold is 2 mA and the LED renders clearly lit
findings.problem: The 'dim' fault is three 470 Ω blocks. On 12 V that gives 7.1 mA, which the story calls 'Barely glowing. The player says it looks broken.' The game's own threshold for 'too dim to see' is 2 mA (HOUSE.lit), the bench renders the 7 mA LED as a bright saturated red with a halo, and the setup passes the play test as 'Works'. A modern 5 mm LED is clearly visible at 1–2 mA. The story teaches a wrong rule of thumb (that an LED below about 8 mA looks broken) and contradicts the meter and the visuals.
findings.fix: Frame the band as matching the other cabinets ('Dimmer than the other cabinets'), not as 'broken'. Choose the 'dim' start so iLoad < band[0]·0.5 (add 470s until true, or pick from chains), so the difference is visible. Scale LED visual brightness with log(current), so 7 mA vs 12 mA is a visible but not dramatic step.
findings.verify: Rerun jobs.mjs: every 'dim' job has startI < band[0]/2. Retake shot 20 and compare with the in-band LED.
findings.verify_reason: The 'dim' start is always 3×470 (logic.ts:216). On 12 V red it gives 7.09 mA, and shot arcade-rush-teach-20 (viewed) shows a clearly lit, saturated red LED with a halo while the story says 'Barely glowing… looks broken'. It then signs off as 'Works'. This is partly true by supply: of 403 dim jobs, 123 are under the 2 mA 'too dim to see' threshold (tier 0, 5 V and 3.3 V), where the story fits. 265/403 already have startI < band[0]/2. The story is false mainly on 9–12 V.

findings.title: 'Backwards' cabinets on 9 V and 12 V put the LED beyond a typical 5 V reverse rating, but the game says it simply 'stays dark'
findings.problem: The 'backwards' fault is generated on any supply (jobs 11, 12, 14 with this seed are 12 V and 9 V). The rule says a reversed LED just stays dark. Typical 5 mm LED datasheets give a maximum reverse voltage of 5 V. On 9 or 12 V a reversed LED is past its rating; the series resistor limits the breakdown current, but this is outside spec. 'Stays dark' is right in what is seen, but it teaches that reversing an LED is always harmless on any supply.
evidence: jobs.mjs output jobs 11, 12, 14 (12 V / 9 V backwards)
findings.fix: Restrict the 'backwards' fault to supply ≤ 5 V in rushJob. Or, when reversed on a supply above 5 V, add a tier-0 note: 'Backwards on 12 V is past a typical LED's 5 V reverse rating; it may fail.'
findings.verify: Unit test: no rush job with start.reversed has supply > 5, or its judge note mentions the reverse rating.
findings.verify_reason: Confirmed that 234/416 (56%) of 'backwards' rush jobs are on 9 or 12 V, so the reversed LED sees the full supply (read() vLoad=V, logic.ts:127). Typical 5 mm LED datasheets list VR = 5 V max. In practice the series resistor limits any breakdown current and many LEDs survive, so 'stays dark' is the truthful observed result. The teaching harm is small: it is an omitted caveat, not a false statement.

findings.title: The same numbers appear three times, and the Vf the player needs is the smallest text on screen
findings.problem: At the bench, the current shows on the side-panel 'Current' row, the meter's CURRENT tile and the LIGHT bar's right label. Chain Ω and hottest-block power each appear on both the panel and the meter. Meanwhile the LED's forward voltage, the one input needed to predict the current (I = (V − Vf)/R), appears only in the meter footer 'SUPPLY 9 V · LED Vf 3.0 V'. That footer is drawn at 22 px on a 900 px canvas and shows about 9 px tall at 1440×900. In rush the LED colour changes every cabinet, so this tiny value is what a predicting player must find each time.
evidence: src/stations/arcade/station.ts:553-572, :579-580 (meter tiles, bar labels, footer FONT 22)
findings.fix: Strip the side panel to the ask, the story and the parts cost, and keep live numbers on the meter only. Print Vf on the board under the LED (drawBoard, station.ts:533) at the same 48 px as the supply ('Vf 3.0 V' in LED colour), so V and Vf both sit on the board beside the chain. Raise the meter labels to ≥ 30 px.
findings.verify: Bench crop: each value appears once, and 'Vf 3.0 V' has a cap height of at least 14 px at 1440×900.
findings.verify_reason: Shots arcade-rush-teach-04/-20/-22 (viewed): current appears on the panel 'Current' row, the meter CURRENT tile and the LIGHT bar's right label. Chain and hottest block appear on both the panel and the meter. Vf appears only in the meter footer (station.ts:579-581, FONT 22 on a 900×520 canvas mapped onto a 1.32 m screen), which renders as tiny text ('SUPPLY 9 V · LED Vf 3.0 V'). The duplication part repeats research-external F5 (research-external.md:147-149). The Vf legibility point is new.
extra_evidence: src/stations/arcade/station.ts:525 (only supply printed on board at 48 px)

findings.title: Naming and doc drift: 'Orders served', 'broken a new way', and the 4-second soak in the docs
findings.problem: The result card says 'Orders served' (carried over from the cut Via Rush). The panel says 'N fixed' and the bonus says 'Eight cabinets or more'. The level tagline promises 'Every cabinet is broken a new way', but there are 5 fault templates, 14 % of starts already 'Work', and the fix set repeats (11 distinct answers). PROGRESS.md still says 'a 4-second soak each' and 'fixable reliably from the rack', but RUSH_SOAK is 2 s and the rack was replaced by bins (AR1 doc conflict still open).
findings.fix: Add a `noun` to rushStatus() ('Cabinets fixed') and use it in game-ui.ts:217. Change the tagline to 'Three minutes. Fix as many cabinets as you can.' (docs edits are for the implementer, not this review): PROGRESS l.215 → '2-second play test', 'from the bins'.
findings.verify: Result card shows 'Cabinets fixed: N'; grep 'Orders served' in src returns nothing.
findings.verify_reason: game-ui.ts:217 'Orders served'. arcade.ts:31 tagline 'Every cabinet is broken a new way': there are 5 fault templates and 11 distinct fixes. PROGRESS.md:215-216 says '4-second soak' (RUSH_SOAK=2, station.ts:24), 'from the rack' (bins now) and 'Every generated cabinet starts broken' (14% start as tier-1 Works). Screenshot arcade-rush-teach-43 shows 'Orders served: 0'.

notes.teaching: Arcade Rush gets the core relation right. I = (V − Vf)/(R + 1 Ω), series sum, parallel combine and polarity all check out in logic.ts. The chain socket is a real mechanic: the player stands blocks in positions, and the CHAIN Ω tile plus the LIGHT band with its ★ zone are visible before power, so prediction is possible. As a drill, though, rush mostly fails to make the player apply the idea. About 35 % of cabinets need no resistor choice: 14 % can be signed off as found, and 21 % are a flip-only ★. The stories print the diagnosis ('block across the LED', 'went in backwards'). Free hot-swapping with an instant meter makes hill-climbing beat computing: a random guess is reliable a quarter of the time, and eleven answers cover everything. Heat (P = I²R against ¼ W and the 60 % rule) never binds in rush, so half of the Arcade lesson goes unpractised. Several player-facing texts contradict the physics or the visuals, and these are the most damaging for learning: 'too bright, smells warm' when the fuse trips (67 % of hot cabinets); 'runs hot and dies early' on an instant LED pop; 'barely glowing' at 7 mA beside a brightly lit LED; a PTC that re-arms while powered; and an overdriven LED that renders paler than a correct one. The fixes are concrete: stories derived from read() and symptom-only, a free first look, latching PTC with power-off reset, first-try scoring, and an escalation that brings in heat and battery cabinets.
notes.clarity: The bench reads well at a glance: a big supply label, colour-coded candy blocks with real bands, a clear ★ zone on the LIGHT bar, a TRIP tile and FUSE COOLING. The main clarity failures are these. The prompt is overridden by a stale hover hint ('D Empty: plain wire' through trip, pop and sign-off). 'P Fuse cooling' labels P as something it doesn't do. Values are tripled between the side panel and the monitor, while the Vf input sits in about 9 px footer text. The success feedback (the play-test kid, the cabinet lamp, TILT) is off-camera, so outcomes are learned from a bar and a toast. Results use the 'Orders served' noun, unlike the rest of the room.
notes.fun: The tempo of the core loop is good. A scripted clean player can fix about 40 cabinets in 126 s, and a 2 s play test with a bell and confetti per cabinet gives a pleasant rhythm. But the mode has no stakes: the grade is always A (zero cabinets earned a gold A, a star and a bonus), the cost axis punishes fixing more, and nothing escalates over the three minutes, so there is no reason to replay for mastery. The tray fetch at the start eats the clock with no fun or learning. Tying the grade to cabinets fixed, first-try accuracy and an escalating fault mix would turn it into a real practice game.
notes.playability: The rush plays without errors: every g.close() returned [], and the shift ends on the clock as specified. The friction points are these. Powering on to look is punished as damage on half the cabinets (a free look is needed). The fuse cool-down is a locked wait of up to 2.5 s after the chain is already fixed. The clock runs during a redundant tray carry. The hover-hint prompt can hide the sign-off key. The LED-pop smoke ball briefly covers the LED and meter. All of these are cheap code fixes in station.ts and logic.ts.
notes.models: Out of scope for this dimension. Incidental: the candy blocks, board and meter read well at the bench camera, and the across-slot block stands visibly across the LED. The LED-pop smoke renders as one oversized translucent sphere (filed under visual-bug).

rechecked: AR1 (R3A N4 pattern: rush countdown + count on result card): FIXED. The HUD clock counts down from 2:59 (shot 01), and the result card shows 'Orders served: N' (shot 43). Still open: the noun mismatch, and the PROGRESS.md l.215 '4-second soak' vs RUSH_SOAK=2 doc conflict.

A-1 / A2 (PTC self-reset): STILL OPEN as a truth problem. The fuse re-arms while powered and re-trips (rush.mjs log, 3.2 s after power-on still tripped; shot 26). Real PPTCs latch until power is removed (Littelfuse paper).

A3 (LED over-rating 'cooked in 2 s'): FIXED in logic (pop only above 2.5×). The visual 'white-hot' flicker now makes an overdriven LED read paler than a correct one (shot 20 vs 22), and the pop toast reuses 'dies early' (shot 23). Filed.
A7 (experiments graded as damage): STILL OPEN and worse in rush. 50 % of generated starts trip on power-on, and the first look costs a mistake and a trip (rush.mjs log job0).

A8 (messages say why, never the fix): STILL OPEN. Toasts print formulas ('(I = (V − Vf) ÷ R)', shot 23), and the rush stories name the fault/fix outright ('went in backwards', 'block across the LED').
A10 (confetti through the bench camera): PARTIAL. Confetti pieces still cross the top of the bench view after sign-off (shots 22, 27), but they don't cover the board.
A11 (stale toast after sitting): FIXED. No stale toast on sitting. The previous cabinet's sign-off toast shows for about 4 s over the next cabinet, which is acceptable.
DR-31 (predict before power): PASS in part. CHAIN Ω and the LIGHT band/★ zone show before power (shot 03), but Vf is in about 9 px footer text, and prediction is never rewarded.
DR-80 (no console errors): PASS. Every arcade-rush-teach script's g.close() returned [].
